---
title: "This is why the EU–Canada alliance matters"
subtitle: |
  The most important thing about the proposed alliance is not what it is called. It is that Canada and Europe are choosing to define it themselves.
categories: [politics, Europe, Canada, European Union, geopolitics, 2026]
date: "2026-09-17"
---

A new political relationship is proposed. It does not yet exist in law. Its institutions have not been designed. Its terms have not been negotiated.

And apparently this is confusing.

That was one of the stranger reactions to Ursula von der Leyen’s proposal that Canada become the European Union’s first “associate member.” [CBC News](https://youtu.be/7uUi6Cx94JA?is=Lmuyd8QEXOTEYEFw) spent much of its coverage explaining that there is no such legal category, that Canada cannot become an ordinary EU member because it is not European, and that von der Leyen cannot simply impose a new arrangement on the Union’s 27 member states.

All true. And almost spectacularly beside the point.

Of course associate membership does not already exist. **She was proposing to create it.**

This is how politics works. Political actors decide that existing arrangements are inadequate, state an objective, negotiate the details, and—if they can assemble the necessary coalition—turn it into law.

Europe did not wake up after the Second World War to discover the European Coal and Steel Community conveniently waiting in a treaty book. The [Schuman Declaration of 9 May 1950](https://european-union.europa.eu/principles-countries-history/history-eu/1945-59/schuman-declaration-may-1950_en) proposed something new: the political principles came first; a treaty and negotiated implementation followed.

The interesting question is not where “associate membership” appears in the current rulebook. It is **what Canada and Europe are trying to build, and whether they can muster the political will to build it.**

Von der Leyen used her [2026 State of the Union address](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RfYjukF1Pe8) to argue that Europe must become more capable of acting on its own behalf in an increasingly dangerous world. In the [official transcript](https://cyprus.representation.ec.europa.eu/news/2026-state-union-address-president-von-der-leyen-2026-09-16_en), she spoke about democratic states choosing their partners, reducing strategic dependencies, and deepening cooperation with Canada in defence, technology, energy, critical minerals and the Arctic.

Then she proposed taking the relationship to the “highest level possible” and opening the door to Canada as the EU’s first associate member.

[The European Parliament stood and applauded.](https://www.reuters.com/world/eu-opens-door-canada-become-first-associate-member-eu-commission-president-says-2026-09-16/)

That did not ratify a treaty. Nobody serious thinks it did. But dismissing it as “just symbolic” manages to misunderstand both symbolism and politics at once. A parliament standing behind an unprecedented proposal sends a message to governments, to Canada, and to other countries watching.

**Europe and Canada are asserting their ability to choose one another.**

That should be an utterly mundane proposition. Donald Trump’s response demonstrated why it is not.

Asked about the proposed relationship, he called it “laughable” and warned that if he considered it a hostile act, the United States could impose very serious tariffs on Europe or stop trading with it in certain areas. [The Associated Press reported the threat directly](https://apnews.com/article/4078e9549ff9caa5ded08f7dd2f99065).

Think about what that means. Canada and Europe consider changing the relationship between themselves, and the president of a third country immediately raises the possibility of economic punishment depending on whether he approves of their intentions.

There could hardly be a more concise demonstration of the strategic problem that “autonomy” is supposed to address. Threatening countries because they are trying to reduce their vulnerability to economic coercion does not weaken the argument for diversification.

It illustrates it.

The Canadian media reaction was revealing in a different way. CBC’s chief political correspondent described the announcement as “confusing” and said von der Leyen’s declaration had “thrown a lot of us off guard.”

This is particularly strange because the basic idea was already public. On September 13, [Reuters reported](https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/carney-pushes-idea-making-canada-associate-member-eu-wsj-reports-2026-09-13/) that Mark Carney had explicitly ruled out ordinary EU membership while saying Canada would begin discussions for a “unique alliance” with the Union. That report followed [The Wall Street Journal’s account](https://www.wsj.com/economy/canada-seeks-eu-associate-member-status-as-u-s-trade-talks-collapse-4eebec65) that an unprecedented form of associate status was being explored.

Those are not contradictory statements. Canada can decline conventional membership of an existing institution while negotiating a new relationship with it.

Yet much of the CBC discussion seemed trapped inside the existing categories. There is only one kind of membership. Canada cannot have that kind. The proposed alternative does not currently exist. Therefore the whole thing is murky, perhaps merely symbolic, perhaps not terribly realistic.

It is politics interpreted as taxonomy.

The most charitable explanation may also be the most interesting: the idea had been reported, but nobody really believed it. It was treated as speculation because it did not fit comfortably within the existing map of the world. Then von der Leyen stood before the European Parliament and made it a political proposal.

The failure was not necessarily one of information. It may have been a failure of imagination.

For decades, Canada has been deeply economically integrated with the United States. European security has rested heavily on American military power. American technology companies dominate much of the digital infrastructure on which both depend. Washington has been so central to the Western political system that its centrality can begin to look less like an arrangement of power and more like a feature of reality.

Under those circumstances, European “strategic autonomy” can sound like rhetoric right up until Europe starts exercising it. Canadian diversification can sound like branding right up until Canada begins constructing relationships that reduce its reliance on the United States.

None of this makes the negotiations easy. The ovation did not tell us what France will demand, how regulatory alignment might work, whether mobility rights will be included, or what Hungary may decide to obstruct on any given Tuesday. Twenty-seven democratic states do not suddenly acquire one opinion because Ursula von der Leyen gives a good speech.

Europe’s distributed authority can make it maddeningly slow. The Commission proposes. Governments negotiate. Parliament participates. National interests collide. Lawyers descend. Years pass.

But that makes agenda-setting more important, not less. Von der Leyen was doing what political leadership in this system requires: stating where she believes Europe should go and attempting to build the coalition that can take it there.

Carney had already framed the objective explicitly. On September 15, he said Canada was deepening ties with trusted partners to increase its [“strategic autonomy”](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/speeches/2026/09/15/prime-minister-carney-delivers-opening-remarks-canada-investment-summit), because “integration has been weaponised” and arrangements work when partners respect one another’s sovereignty.

After their meeting in Strasbourg, the Canadian government described a move beyond CETA toward a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance” across defence, AI and compute, energy, space, critical minerals, financial infrastructure and digital trade. Ottawa called it [“a unique approach that they will define together”](https://www.pm.gc.ca/en/news/readouts/2026/09/16/prime-minister-carney-meets-president-european-commission-ursula-von-der).

That last phrase answers much of the confusion. The arrangement has not been defined because defining it is the work they are proposing to do. [Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/teu_2012/art_49/oj/eng) governs ordinary accession by a European state; [Article 217](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2012/art_217/oj/eng) already allows association agreements with third countries. What this relationship ultimately requires will depend on what Canada and Europe want it to contain.

It may be watered down. Governments may block important elements. Economic realities may constrain both sides. “Associate membership” may disappear and leave behind agreements with a more conventional name.

But the political declaration has happened. Europe’s leadership has proposed an unprecedented relationship, Canada has welcomed it, and Europe’s elected parliament has stood behind the idea.

The most consequential statement von der Leyen made was not “associate membership.” It was the principle immediately surrounding it: democratic countries must be free to choose whom they work with.

Canada and Europe have now begun to act as though they believe that principle.

Whatever legal structure eventually emerges, **that assertion of agency is already real.**
